name: Robert L. Bradshaw International Airport
before:
The airport for St Kitts, just north east of Basseterre, and capable of a good deal more than its size suggests. Non-stop jet services run to Canada and the United States alongside the regional Caribbean commuter flights, and the apron takes six wide bodied aircraft at once. The largest aircraft to have landed here is a Boeing 747-400.

That capacity is recent. The airport was built in the 1940s and the runway, now 2,439 metres, was completely resurfaced as part of a seventeen million dollar programme finished in December 2006, which also widened the apron and added a taxiway.

It handles cargo and private jets as well as scheduled traffic. Passenger numbers were just under 400,000 in 2008.

It is named after Robert Llewellyn Bradshaw, the first Premier of what was then St Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla, and was called Golden Rock Airport before that, which is the name older guides use.
after:
The airport for St Kitts, just north east of Basseterre. Non-stop jet services run to the United States and, in winter, to Canada, alongside regional Caribbean flights.

It is named after Robert Llewellyn Bradshaw and was called Golden Rock Airport before that, which is the name older guides use.

claims.note: The government's own fact page lists one airport per island: Robert L. Bradshaw on St Kitts, Vance W. Amory on Nevis.

claims.inAfter: It is named after Robert Llewellyn Bradshaw
claims.note: Was 'named after Robert Llewellyn Bradshaw, the first Premier of what was then St Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla'. The government lists the airport under his name and Sir Robert L. Bradshaw as one of the National Heroes, but gives no titles, so 'first Premier' rests on Wikipedia alone (cut below). The government pages do not say in words that the airport is named after him; the name itself and Wikipedia's statement carry it.

claims.claim: all visitors need an Electronic Travel Authorisation
claims.why: Held back: a verified fact that replaces nothing in the old text. The FCDO (updated 5 January 2026) says all visitors to St Kitts and Nevis must get an eTA before travel, and the government's 2026 Budget Address describes the launch of the eTA system. Worth adding if Andy agrees, as it will catch a traveller out.

claims.why: Held back: replaces nothing (the old text names no UK service). The UK CAA's 2025 route table has 22,239 scheduled passengers between Gatwick and St Kitts in 2025 (20,078 in 2024), and the Nevis Tourism Authority lists Gatwick to St Kitts on Tuesdays and Saturdays. Neither names the airline in the saved text, and the tourism authority's 'nonstop' is marketing copy that no airline source was read to confirm, so the airline and any stop would need the airline's own page before this goes in.
